title: Bhutan for Indian travellers: permits, SDF and documents
summary: Indian nationals need no visa for Bhutan. Carry a valid passport or original voter ID, pay the Sustainable Development Fee of ₹1,200 per person per night, stay in certified hotels and take a licensed guide beyond Thimphu and Paro. Entry permits are issued online, at Phuentsholing or at Paro airport; route permits for other districts come from Thimphu.
meta_description: Bhutan rules for Indians: passport or voter ID, ₹1,200 SDF, entry and route permits, guide and hotel rules, money and etiquette. Indicative; check current.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Bhutan treats Indian visitors as regional tourists. You do not need a visa, and you pay a much lower daily fee than other nationalities. But since Bhutan reopened after the pandemic in September 2022, the rules have been tighter than many people remember from earlier trips, when Indians could drive in and wander freely.

Today every Indian tourist needs an entry permit, pays the Sustainable Development Fee (SDF) for each night in the country, stays only in accommodation certified by the Department of Tourism, and travels with a licensed Bhutanese guide outside Thimphu and Paro. None of this is hard to arrange, but it shapes the cost and the plan of any trip.

This guide sets out what we know from planning trips in 2025 and 2026. Bhutan revises its tourism rules from time to time, sometimes at short notice, so treat everything here as indicative. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Documents you need
paras: Indian adults can enter Bhutan with either of two documents. The first is a valid Indian passport with at least six months' validity from the date of entry. The second is an original voter ID card, the EPIC issued by the Election Commission of India. Photocopies and digital copies are not accepted in place of the original.

Other Indian documents do not work. Aadhaar, PAN cards, driving licences and ration cards are not accepted as travel documents, even though people sometimes report otherwise on social media. Children under 18 who have neither a passport nor a voter ID can travel with a birth certificate, accompanied by a parent or legal guardian; some travellers also carry a school identity card.
Carry the following in a single folder so the immigration office can process you quickly:
list: Original passport or voter ID for every adult, and a passport or birth certificate for each child
Two recent passport-size photographs per person
Confirmed bookings in certified hotels for your nights in Bhutan
Your itinerary, and your guide's or operator's details if you are going beyond Thimphu and Paro
A printout of your online permit if you applied in advance

sections.heading: The Sustainable Development Fee
paras: The SDF is a nightly fee that Bhutan charges every tourist to fund conservation, health, education and the offsetting of tourism's impact. For Indian nationals it is ₹1,200 per person per night, payable in rupees or ngultrum. It is collected when your permit is issued, for the number of nights you plan to stay.

Children aged 6 to 12 pay half, ₹600 a night, and children under 6 do not pay. Other nationalities pay USD 100 per person per night, a reduced rate introduced in 2023 and set to last for some years; they also need a visa. Bangladeshi and Maldivian nationals have their own regional arrangements.

The fee is per night spent in Bhutan, not per day. That matters for overland travellers: a night in Jaigaon on the Indian side, or in Jaldapara, attracts no SDF. Day visitors to Phuentsholing town have generally been exempt, but border-town rules have been revised more than once. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Entry permits and route permits
paras: The entry permit is the basic document for an Indian tourist. It allows travel in Thimphu and Paro districts. You can apply online in advance through the Department of Immigration's portal, or get it in person at the regional immigration office near the gate in Phuentsholing, or on arrival at Paro International Airport. Applying online in advance saves time, especially in busy months.

At Phuentsholing, the office is open on weekdays and part of Saturday, and closed on Sundays and Bhutanese public holidays. Arrive early with your documents and bookings; on busy days in May, June and October there can be long queues. The permit is usually issued the same day.

To go beyond Thimphu and Paro, to Punakha, Wangdue Phodrang for Phobjikha, Haa, Bumthang or elsewhere, you need a route permit for each district. It is issued by the immigration office in Thimphu or applied for online, and your licensed guide or tour operator normally handles it. Plan to be in Thimphu on a working day if the permit is to be issued there. Checkpoints along the highways inspect permits.

sections.heading: Guides, hotels and vehicles
paras: Since 2022 all tourists, including Indians, must be accompanied by a licensed Bhutanese guide when travelling beyond Thimphu and Paro, and on any trek. Within Thimphu and Paro you may move about on your own, take taxis and public buses, and visit sights, although some monuments may ask for a guide at the entrance. A licensed guide typically costs ₹2,500–3,500 a day for the group, plus their food and lodging on overnight trips.

You must also stay in accommodation certified by the Department of Tourism. That includes approved hotels from simple to luxury, and registered farmhouse homestays. Unregistered guesthouses and staying with friends are not allowed for tourists. Certified budget hotels in Thimphu and Paro start around ₹2,500–3,500 a room a night.

Indian-registered private vehicles can enter Bhutan with a vehicle permit and a daily fee, and the driver needs a valid licence and documents. Most Indian taxis do not go beyond the border. In practice most visitors switch to a Bhutan-registered car with a driver, usually booked with the guide, or use public buses between Phuentsholing, Thimphu and Paro. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Money, phones and time
paras: The ngultrum is pegged to the Indian rupee at par, and rupees are accepted across Bhutan. Carry ₹100 and ₹200 notes; some shops and taxis refuse ₹500 notes, a hangover from older restrictions on large Indian notes. UPI works at many shops in Thimphu, Paro and Phuentsholing through a cross-border link, and ATMs of Bhutanese banks accept some Indian cards, but cash is safer in the villages.

Indian SIM cards on international roaming work in the main towns but can be costly. A local SIM from B-Mobile or TashiCell costs a few hundred rupees with data and needs your permit and ID. Coverage is good on main roads and in towns, patchy in valleys such as Phobjikha and Haa.

Bhutan Time is 30 minutes ahead of Indian Standard Time. Government offices, including immigration, and buses run to Bhutan Time. Tuesday is a dry day across the country, when bars and alcohol shops are closed.

sections.heading: Etiquette and rules that surprise visitors
paras: Bhutan has strict rules on tobacco. Smoking in public places is banned, and sales are controlled; if you carry cigarettes for personal use, keep the quantity small and expect to show them at customs. Drones need prior permission. Photography is not allowed inside temples and dzong shrine rooms.

Dress matters in religious and government buildings. Wear long sleeves, long trousers or a long skirt, and no caps inside dzongs and temples. Walk clockwise around chortens, prayer wheels and temples. Do not point your feet at altars, and do not touch religious objects without being invited.

Finally, be patient with the system. Rules exist because Bhutan chose to limit tourism's effect on a small country. Indian travellers still pay far less than anyone else, and a well-planned trip runs smoothly. Check current status before you travel, and keep your permit and ID with you at all times.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a visa for Bhutan?
faqs.a: No. Indian nationals need only an entry permit, issued online or at Phuentsholing or Paro airport. Carry a valid passport with six months' validity or an original voter ID card. Other nationalities need a visa arranged in advance. Rules are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Aadhaar accepted for entry into Bhutan?
faqs.a: No. Aadhaar, PAN cards and driving licences are not accepted as travel documents for Bhutan. Adults need a valid passport or an original voter ID card. Children under 18 without these can use a birth certificate and must travel with a parent or guardian. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much SDF do Indian children pay?
faqs.a: Children aged 6 to 12 pay half the SDF, ₹600 per night, and children under 6 pay nothing. From 13 they pay the full adult rate of ₹1,200 per night. Carry a birth certificate or passport so ages can be confirmed at immigration. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I apply for the Bhutan permit online?
faqs.a: Yes. The Department of Immigration runs an online portal for entry permits, and tour operators can apply on your behalf. You upload your ID, photo and hotel bookings and pay the SDF. You can still get the permit in person at Phuentsholing or Paro airport, but online saves time in busy months.

faqs.q: What is a route permit in Bhutan?
faqs.a: A route permit lets you travel to districts beyond Thimphu and Paro, such as Punakha, Wangdue Phodrang for Phobjikha, Haa or Bumthang. It is issued by the immigration office in Thimphu or online, usually through your licensed guide. Checkpoints on the highways inspect it, so keep it with you.

faqs.q: Can I drive my own car from India into Bhutan?
faqs.a: Indian-registered private vehicles can enter with a vehicle permit and a daily fee, and the driver must carry a valid licence, registration and insurance. You still need a licensed guide beyond Thimphu and Paro. Many travellers find a Bhutanese car and driver simpler. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide in Thimphu and Paro?
faqs.a: Not for moving around. Tourists may explore Thimphu and Paro on their own, using taxis and public buses. Some monuments may ask for a guide at the entrance, and many visitors hire one for Taktsang and the dzongs. Beyond these two districts, a licensed guide is compulsory.

faqs.q: Is the SDF charged for nights in Jaigaon?
faqs.a: No. The SDF applies only to nights spent in Bhutan. Jaigaon is in India, so a night there costs nothing extra beyond the hotel. Many budget travellers stay in Jaigaon on arrival or departure, crossing into Phuentsholing during the day, to save one or two nights of SDF.

faqs.q: Are hotel bookings checked when the permit is issued?
faqs.a: Yes. Immigration asks for confirmed bookings in certified accommodation for your nights in Bhutan. Your operator can provide these if they arrange your stay. Turning up without bookings can delay the permit, especially in May, June and October. Keep printed or digital copies handy.
